papers.title: Exploration of tumor genomics associated with prolonged benefit from or resistance to talazoparib monotherapy in patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer.
papers.abstract: Poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibition is synthetically lethal in cells with deleterious alterations in DNA damage response genes involved in homologous recombination repair (HRR). Alterations in HRR genes, including BRCA1/2, have been identified in ~25% of prostate cancer samples and linked with worse clinical outcomes. We explored relationships between tumor genetics and prolonged benefit with talazoparib in TALAPRO-1. The phase II TALAPRO-1 trial evaluated talazoparib monotherapy in pretreated patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer with HRR gene alterations. Tumor genetics were retrospectively assessed in subgroups in the efficacy population (n = 104) based on radiographic progression-free survival (rPFS: ≥12 months; ≥2 to <12 months; <2 months). Serial circulating tumor DNA samples from weeks 1, 9, and 25 and the safety follow-up visit (SFUV) were assessed for emergent changes in mutational profiles using FoundationOne®Liquid CDx. Among 16 patients with rPFS ≥ 12 months, 15 (94%) exhibited tumor BRCA2 alterations vs. 6/27 (22%) patients with rPFS < 2 months (p < 0.00001). HRR gene reversions predicted to restore HRR gene function were detected in 7/27 patients (BRCA1 [n = 1], BRCA2 [n = 5], PALB2 [n = 1]) evaluable for emergent variants at week 25 and/or the SFUV. Emergent PARP1 variants predicted to truncate PARP1 and/or inhibit talazoparib binding were evident in 5/27 evaluable patients. Patients experiencing prolonged benefit typically exhibited tumor BRCA2 copy number loss. Reversion mutations of HRR genes and emergent PARP1 variants likely reflect selective pressure to escape talazoparib synthetic lethality and/or PARP trapping. NCT03148795.

papers.title: Molecular characteristics and clinical outcomes of ERBB2-activating mutation-positive non-small cell lung cancer: A Japanese nationwide real-world cohort.
papers.abstract: Erb-b2 receptor tyrosine kinase 2 (ERBB2)-activating mutations are well-documented oncogenic drivers in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), occurring in approximately 1-4% of cases. These alterations include a heterogeneous spectrum of variant subtypes; however, the clinicogenomic characteristics and clinical significance of the individual variants have yet to be elucidated. We searched the nationwide Center for Cancer Genomics and Advanced Therapeutics database, which integrates comprehensive genome profiling data generated in routine clinical practice across Japan, to investigate the molecular landscape and clinical outcomes of patients with ERBB2-mutated NSCLC. A total of 319 patients with ERBB2-activating mutations were included in this retrospective analysis. Although 74% of the patients harbored canonical tyrosine kinase domain (TKD) in-frame insertions, 26% carried noncanonical variants, including TKD missense (8%), transmembrane/juxtamembrane domain (10%), and extracellular domain (ECD) mutations (8%). Co-occurring oncogenic driver alterations were identified in only 18 cases (5.6%) and were largely restricted to noncanonical variants, whereas no co-occurring driver alterations were detected among patients with TKD in-frame mutations. Noncanonical variants-TKD missense and ECD mutations in particular-were associated with an increased tumor mutational burden. Among 288 patients with available survival data, 78 (27%) received trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) during their clinical course. After excluding patients who had started treatment with T-DXd before undergoing comprehensive genome profiling testing, time-dependent T-DXd exposure was associated with a reduced risk of death (adjusted hazard ratio, 0.63; 95% confidence interval, 0.39-1.01; P = 0.057). ERBB2-mutated NSCLC exhibited substantial molecular heterogeneity, with canonical TKD in-frame insertions characterized by a low frequency of co-occurring oncogenic driver alterations. Among patients harboring ERBB2-activating mutations, exposure to T-DXd was associated with improved overall survival.

papers.title: Development of an hAPE1-Based RT-RAA Method for Rapid Detection of Sweet Potato Chlorotic Stunt Virus.
papers.abstract: Sweet potato chlorotic stunt virus (SPCSV) is a major pathogen that threatens sweet potato production. It frequently acts synergistically with other viruses, causing severe yield losses and quality decline. A rapid and efficient detection method is therefore essential for preventing and controlling the spread of this virus. Here, we developed a reverse transcription real-time fluorescence recombinase-aided amplification (RT-RAA) assay using human apurinic/apyrimidinic endonuclease 1 (hAPE1, designated as tool enzyme E10). This enzyme exhibits high apurinic/apyrimidinic endonuclease activity but extremely low exonuclease activity, so that amplification products remain intact rather than being degraded, as commonly occurs with the traditionally used exonuclease III (ExoIII), thereby preserving product integrity for subsequent analysis. The established RT-hAPE1-RAA assay for SPCSV can be completed within 10 min and has a sensitivity of 100 ag/μl, corresponding to approximately 26 copies/μl of a recombinant pUC57 plasmid (3,484 bp) containing a 774-bp SPCSV coat protein gene. Gel electrophoresis confirmed that E10 preserved viral amplification fragments intact, whereas ExoIII caused significant degradation. When testing 43 field-collected sweet potato samples, the method demonstrated a sensitivity of 94.4% and a specificity of 100%, showing high concordance with reverse transcription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) results. Furthermore, E10 maintained stable cleavage activity across diverse target sequences, indicating its broad applicability. This work provides a rapid, sensitive, and reliable tool for SPCSV detection and offers technical support for the on-site diagnosis of sweet potato viral diseases.

papers.title: Targeted siRNA screening coupled with unbiased proteomics identify potassium signaling as a critical regulator of pigmentation
papers.abstract: Ion channels are emerging as critical regulators of cellular signaling, influencing diverse pathophysiological processes and offering promising opportunities for therapeutic intervention. However, the contribution of ionic homeostasis to human skin pigmentation remains poorly understood. Here, we identify potassium (K+) dynamics as a critical regulator of pigmentation and uncover K+ channel Kir7.1 as a molecular link between K+ and cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) signaling. A targeted siRNA screen identified six previously unrecognized regulators of pigmentation, which we validated using mouse cell line systems, primary human melanocytes, and an in vivo zebrafish model. Unbiased proteomic analyses of two prominent screening hits, Rhot1 and VDAC3, led us to identify Kir7.1, a plasma membrane-localized K+ channel, as a key determinant of pigmentation. Integrating cellular, molecular, ultrastructural, and microscopy approaches, we demonstrate functional crosstalk between the hits and Kir7.1 channel activity. Mechanistically, Kir7.1 promotes the canonical cAMP-protein kinase A (PKA) pathway, establishing this channel as a molecular node that couples K+ dynamics to the classical melanogenic pathway. Notably, Kir7.1 is differentially expressed in skin pigmentary disorders such as vitiligo and melasma, highlighting its therapeutic potential. Taken together, our findings establish Kir7.1 as an important regulator of skin pigmentation and reveal an unanticipated connection between K+ homeostasis, mitochondrial Ca2+ handling toolkit, and cAMP-dependent melanogenesis. This work provides a foundation for exploring K+ signaling as a potential therapeutic avenue for human pigmentary disorders.

papers.title: SMSTPred: Protein Language Model Embeddings Predict SAM-Methyltransferase Substrate Specificity and Reveal Metabolite Methyltransferasome Enrichment in Plants and Actinomycetota
papers.abstract: S-adenosyl-methionine (SAM)-dependent methyltransferases (MTases) are one of the largest and most ancient enzyme superfamilies in biology, transferring a methyl group from SAM to substrates as different as DNA, RNA, proteins, and small-molecule metabolites. Most SAM-MTases share a Class I Rossmann-like SAM-binding core, with substrate specificity determined by variable inserts and accessory domains rather than the conserved fold; as a result, substrate type is unknown for most MTases in sequence databases, which are dominated by unreviewed entries. Here we present SMSTPred (SAM-Methyltransferase Substrate-Type Predictor), a multi-label classifier that predicts MTase substrate type from protein language model embeddings and benchmarks it under homology-disjoint cross-validation against sequence-homology, structure-homology, and profile-HMM baselines. SMSTPred reaches a cluster-disjoint Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) of 0.94, significantly ahead of sequence-homology (MMseqs2, 0.85), structure-homology (Foldseek, 0.89) and profile-HMM (0.52) baselines, while providing calibrated, per-substrate confidence. Applying it to ~116,000 MTases across 1,249 reference proteomes, we map the substrate landscape of methylation across the tree of life. Substrate specialization tracks taxonomy: animals expand protein- and DNA-methylation, whereas small-molecule methyltransferases are enriched in plants and Actinomycetota; in Actinomycetota beyond what is expected for their proteome size, and in plants in proportion to their larger proteomes. The predictions identify thousands of uncharacterized methyltransferases with substrate type assignments (about half of those in uncharacterized clusters), many corroborated by an independent reaction-retrieval method. Notably, ~11% of enzymes with a single substrate call lack any class-discriminative sequence motif, suggesting that substrate specificity is often encoded beyond short linear motifs. Together, this work provides SMSTPred, a substrate-type predictor for Class I methyltransferases, and a tree-of-life resource of testable functional hypotheses.

papers.title: Mathematical genomics of hidden signatures in NCF1: implications for chronic granulomatous disease
papers.abstract: Inborn errors of immunity (IEIs), such as Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD), impose a disproportionately severe clinical burden in populations with high rates of consanguinity. CGD is caused by defects in the phagocyte NADPH oxidase complex, frequently due to mutations in the NCF1 gene encoding the p47phox protein. While the functional domains of NCF1 are well characterized, the quantitative architectural constraints governing its structural stability remain elusive. This study aimed to decipher the multidimensional quantitative signatures of NCF1, across diverse organisms in order to understand its conserved spatial sequence architecture and the structural basis of variant severity. We analyzed 41 NCF1 sequences using ten distinct quantitative features, integrating primary sequence metrics, biophysical chemistry, and abstract topological geometry. The synthesis of these features revealed a lack of a unified proximity matrix, demonstrating that NCF1 is defined by feature-dependent, multidimensional individual signatures. Primary sequence metrics exhibited rigid phylogenetic conservation, revealing invariant zero-entropy blocks that correlated strictly with severe CGD-causing mutations, while topological metrics exposed a deep spatial architectural convergence. These multidimensional baselines confirmed that the protein requires a highly specific spatial packing to assemble the NADPH oxidase complex; pathogenic mutations therefore disrupt precise structural signatures rather than globally destroying the protein. Consistent with this, the AlphaFold model places the folded PX and tandem SH3 domains in a high-confidence core and the regulatory C-terminal tail in an exposed, low-confidence region, supporting a tail-mediated autoinhibitory mechanism. Ultimately, this quantitative framework offers a useful perspective on NCF1 architecture and may serve as a supportive tool for evaluating the severity of clinical variants, contributing to precision medicine efforts for NCF1-associated diseases.

papers.title: In vitro and in vivo validation of recombinant Syrian hamster interferon-α
papers.abstract: The Syrian hamster (Mesocricetus auratus) is an important model for the study of viral pathogenesis and the development of antiviral drugs and vaccines, yet species-specific reagents remain scarce. Here, we validate the potent and specific activity of recombinantly expressed Syrian hamster maIFN-12-like protein (maIFN) in vitro and in vivo. MaIFN expressed in E. coli induced MX2 and ISG15 expression in both BHK21 hamster kidney cells as well as in primary hamster fibroblasts in a dose-dependent manner and EC50 values in low pg/mL range. Activation was strictly STAT2-dependent and more potent, by at least one order of magnitude, than that achieved by heterologous human or mouse IFN. ISG induction translated into a strong antiviral activity against YF17D virus replication in BHK21 cells as well as ISRE-dependent reporter expression in a newly established hamster reporter cell line. When tested in wild-type but not in STAT2-deficient hamsters, maIFN showed a physiologic, vigorous yet rapidly contracting systemic ISG response. Together these findings establish maIFN as a functional antiviral cytokine and valuable reagent for preclinical infectious disease research using Syrian hamsters.

papers.title: A Biologically Interpretable Single-Cell Pathology Foundation Model for Molecular Decoding of H&E Images
papers.abstract: The microscopic structure of human tissues encodes molecular information that is not directly accessible by visual inspection. Current pathology foundation models improve histological interpretation but operate at multicellular resolution. It remains unclear whether routine histology contains structured molecular and cellular information recoverable at single-cell resolution, which biological properties are associated with this recoverability, and where its limits lie. Here, we introduce Loki2, a single-cell pathology foundation model trained on UniSeg, a pan-tissue resource integrating 15 million cells with segmentation, lineage annotations and measured or histology-inferred transcriptomic profiles. We examine the above question across cellular representation, molecular recoverability, and patient-level relevance. Loki2 captures cellular identity and continuous morphological variation, with interpretable latent dimensions linked to physical nuclear phenotypes through DAPI validation. Transcriptomic retrieval and in silico protein staining test molecular recoverability, with gene-level analyses revealing the strongest recovery for genes associated with morphologically distinct cellular identities and functions. Then, patient staging and biomarker discovery connect cellular morphology representations to clinical relevance. Together, these findings establish Loki2 as a biologically interpretable single-cell pathology foundation model and provide the opportunities of recovering cellular and molecular information from routine H&E histology at single-cell resolution.

papers.title: Air and environmental sampling expand metagenomic viral surveillance in Cambodian pig slaughterhouses
papers.abstract: Surveillance of viruses in swine depends largely on the sampling of individual animals chosen at random, often limiting detection breadth. Environmental sampling has emerged as an alternative strategy, enabling faster, safer and more cost-effective pathogen monitoring at the human-animal interfaces. Across nine visits to two Cambodian slaughterhouses, we applied metagenomic sequencing to air samples (n = 25), faeces (n = 156), wastewater (n = 15), carcass wash water (n = 18), holding-pen swabs (n = 124), slaughter-box swabs (n = 73) and ropes (n = 16), comparing virus composition to pig snout swabs (n = 193). Combined environmental sampling recovered 96.6% of the viral taxa detected in snout swabs, exceeding 90.9% at every visit. Greater viral diversity was consistently captured in the environment, including swine-associated taxa absent from snout swabs and viral RNA associated with avian and human hosts. Air provided the widest coverage of any single environmental sample type and contributed the largest number of independent virus detections that were not recovered from any other environmental sample. Slaughter-box swabs recovered the fewest taxa, showing that visible contamination with swine material did not correlate with greater viral recovery. Overall, this study identifies air as a pivotal core component of any surveillance program. However, pairing air with additional environmental sample types provides the broadest virus coverage and represents the optimal surveillance strategy in swine slaughterhouses.

papers.title: Mapping the Plant Extracellular Proteome: From Fraction-Specific Secretion Patterns to Experimental Guidelines
papers.abstract: Proteins operating beyond the plasma membrane are central to how plants build and remodel their cell walls, acquire and redistribute nutrients, coordinate developmental processes, and communicate between cells and tissues. Moreover, the reach of this extracellular proteome extends beyond the plant itself, with root and seed exudates shaping the rhizosphere and spermosphere by providing molecular signals and resources that influence microbial communities even before pathogens or symbionts establish direct contact with the plant surface. The extracellular space is therefore a dynamic biological interface connecting processes within the plant to interactions with the soil, microbiome, and broader environment. Despite this central role, the plant extracellular proteome remains fragmented across experimental approaches. Here, we review current techniques for the collection and purification of major plant extracellular fractions and use a uniform prediction pipeline to assess representative publicly available datasets. This analysis reveals consistent fraction-specific patterns in predicted secretion-class composition, with putative unconventional-secretion candidates exceeding canonical candidates in most fractions. We then present a decision tree linking biological questions to appropriate collection and fractionation strategies, together with complementary experimental criteria for assessing extracellular origin that extend beyond sequence-based prediction. Together, these resources provide a framework for interpreting existing extracellular proteomic datasets and for designing future studies that account for the biological distinctness of individual extracellular fractions. They are intended both as an entry point to plant extracellular proteomics and as a reference framework for improving the biological interpretation and comparability of studies across this diverse extracellular landscape.

papers.title: S-PLM-TM enables fast and accurate sequence-based search for remote homologs
papers.abstract: Protein structures and functions can remain conserved after extensive sequence divergence, but detecting these distant relationships across large databases remains challenging. Here we present S-PLM-TM, a sequence-only remote homology search tool based on a structure-aware protein language model. Cross-modal flow matching and contrastive learning incorporate structural information into sequence representations. A lightweight calibration head enables structural-similarity search with the frozen encoder, while a residue-level alignment head generates structural alignments directly from sequence. S-PLM-TM outperforms the tested sequence-based methods in remote homology detection, rivals structure-based methods in structural classification and retrieves the most functionally consistent neighbors. It also retrieves distantly related enzymes with shared catalytic functions at a level comparable to the best-performing structure-based methods. In large-scale database search, S-PLM-TM achieves the highest average precision among both sequence-based and alignment-free methods, with speed approaching the fastest sequence-alignment tools. Together, these results establish S-PLM-TM as a practical tool that combines sensitive and biologically informative remote homology search with the speed required for database-scale retrieval.

papers.title: Quantum Machine Learning for Missense Variant Pathogenicity Prediction in the KCNQ Gene Family
papers.abstract: Missense variants in the KCNQ family of voltage-gated potassium channel genes are associated with a broad spectrum of neurological and cardiac disorders for which computational tools capable of differentiating benign and pathogenic variants are essential. Here, we present, to our knowledge, the first application of quantum machine learning (QML) to missense pathogenicity prediction. We employ a hybrid quantum framework combining data re-uploading quantum neural networks with quantum support vector machines and applied it to pathogenicity classification across the full KCNQ gene family. Systematic exploration of circuit architectures revealed that optimal hyperparameter choices enable the proposed quantum model to achieve predictive performance superior to or comparable to state-of-the-art classical machine learning approaches, reaching AUC-ROC values of approximately 0.94 across the full dataset. Although no clear quantum advantage is observed at present, these results demonstrate that quantum feature representations can effectively capture biologically relevant patterns in variant data and establish QML as a viable framework for future applications in computational genomics and precision medicine.

papers.title: Deciphering the Biological Function of Tandem Mass Spectra Using a Dual-Modal Metabolite Language Model
papers.abstract: Liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry untargeted metabolomics captures thousands of metabolic peaks from biological samples. Conventional identification-dependent metabolomics workflows require confident structural annotation before identified features can enter downstream pathway or functional analysis. However, only a small fraction of detected metabolic features can be assigned confident structural annotations, leaving a large fraction difficult to incorporate into downstream biological interpretation, a form of "functional dark matter". Here, we introduce Spec2Function, a function-centric framework that infers biological functions from tandem mass spectrometry (MS2) spectra. Spec2Function is trained using characterized spectrum-text pairs but does not require prior structural identification of the query spectra at inference time. At its core is Spec2Biotext, a dual-encoder contrastive model that embeds MS2 spectra and curated multi-aspect natural language functional texts into a unified functional space. Combined with a retrieval-augmented generation framework grounded in curated databases and biomedical literature, Spec2Function retrieves evidence-grounded biological knowledge and produces coherent functional summaries for individual spectra or groups of spectra. Across metabolite- and pathway-level benchmarks, Spec2Function achieved higher similarity to reference functional descriptions than the evaluated comparators and expanded the fraction of the metabolome accessible to functional interpretation. Application to a human liver cirrhosis cohort recapitulated known metabolic alterations and identified additional literature-supported functional modules. Applying Spec2Function to a 30-organ macaque aging atlas revealed organ-specific metabolic functions and previously unreported functional modules that were supported by independent human and mouse datasets. Together, these results position Spec2Function as a function-centric framework for scalable biological interpretation of structurally unannotated MS2 spectra.

papers.title: Policy-Enforced Genomic Repositories and Institutional Data Governance for African Pathogen Surveillance with UbuntuBio
papers.abstract: Research centers curating pathogen sequence cohorts often operate under constrained bandwidth, multi-institutional data-sharing agreements, and strict biosafety requirements. Global public archives keep released sequences permanently open, external viral portals enforce terms outside local institutional custody, and standard Git Large File Storage (LFS) duplicates identical binaries across repositories without validating taxonomy or geography. We present UbuntuBio (v1.0.0), a Git-native, policy-enforced genomic repository platform deployed at https://ubuntubio.org and developed at the West African Centre for Cell Biology of Infectious Pathogens (WACCBIP), University of Ghana. UbuntuBio integrates four mechanisms under a single storage root: (1) bare Git repositories storing dataset cards, sample sheets, and approximately 130-byte LFS pointers backed by prefix-sharded SHA-256 content-addressed storage (CAS) with visibility-scoped wire deduplication; (2) a four-phase commit pipeline recoverable via cross-plane reconciliation that enforces 55 African Union country codes against offline Natural Earth polygons, core MIxS-derived fields, Taxon 9606 rejection, and server-keyed targeted human-marker screening identically across HTTP commits and Git pre-receive hooks; (3) institutional custody controls combining Data Use Agreements (DUAs), revocable 900-second RS256 capability tokens, key rotation, tamper-evident hash-chained logs, and externally anchorable RS256 audit checkpoints; and (4) an embedded SQLite WAL and FTS5 catalog filtered by access tier. In single-node evaluation, UbuntuBio classified 18/18 policy boundary fixtures consistently across Python, Git, and HTTP paths; showed 0/265,157 false cross-matches on 21/22 RefSeq pathogen sequences (while cross-matching Candida albicans 18S rDNA at 0.113% and Chlorocebus sabaeus Alu repeats in ENA stool reads, confirming targeted marker detection rather than verified human DNA decontamination); matched conditional uniform (n = 2,000; 200-seed 0.01% convergence 19.0% vs. 18.13% expected) and interior (n = 1,000) detection theory while detecting all spike-ins at [≥] 0.5% (30/30); halved two-repository disk usage on 613.83 MiB Nigerian E. coli runs; passed 27/27 structured-filter correctness checks over 10,000 biosamples and reached graded NDCG@10 = 0.920 on independent free-text BM25 queries with zero private leaks; and recovered cleanly across seven injected phase-transition faults.

papers.title: statLens enables accurate and interpretable statistical intelligence
papers.abstract: Diverse existing approaches and analyses of large-scale biomedical omics datasets along with the complexity of the corresponding statistical analytical workflows pose challenges to the direct application of large language models (LLMs) to data analysis tasks. We present statLens, a model-agnostic AI-driven statistical intelligence framework that integrates LLMs, code and human review. We demonstrate statLens using differential expression analysis across heterogeneous biomedical data as a use case. On 102 benchmark tasks from 74 datasets across six omics modalities, statLens maintained consistently high accuracy (92.5--95.0\%) across seven language models and outperformed LLM-only inference (17.5--46.8\%), whereas autonomous-agent accuracy varied widely (58.7--99.5\%). We also showed that statLens substantially improved the accuracy of the four small language models (92.5--94.4\%) over autonomous agents (58.7--92.2\%) and LLM-only inference (17.5--43.5\%). By decomposing analytical workflows into complementary tasks for code, LLMs and human experts, statLens provides an integrated framework for more accurate, interpretable and reproducible AI-assisted data analysis, particularly in complex omics settings.

papers.title: MINA: Do frozen DNA encoders beat sequence composition? A homology-aware linear-probe benchmark
papers.abstract: Frozen DNA encoders are widely used as feature extractors, but fine-tuning hides what their fixed embeddings already make linearly accessible. MINA is a lightweight benchmark that asks whether those embeddings beat sequence composition, with two linear probes on 3,244 human genes: 5-way classification into coarse protein families, and regression onto each gene's GenePT text-summary embedding. Mostly, they do not. On coding sequence (CDS) under a homology aware split, the validation-selected encoder, NT-v2, recovers coarse family signal at about the level of nucleotide composition (macro-F1 0.693 vs. 0.639; Holm p = 0.108) but does not reach amino-acid composition (0.767) or the protein language model ESM-2 (0.954). On GenePT, DNABERT-2 beats nucleotide composition (R2 0.065 vs. 0.039) but not amino-acid composition (0.080). Evaluation choices move scores as much as the encoder does: pooling alone takes NT-v2 from 0.504, below nucleotide composition, to 0.698; a mostly noncoding transcription-start-site window, where any signal is likely regulatory rather than family, drops NT-v2 from 0.694 to 0.300 on the same genes; and a random split inflates it from 0.693 to 0.801 through homologous genes leaking into the test set. Frozen DNA encoders thus recover little from coding sequence beyond nucleotide composition, and fair comparisons must use composition baselines and fix pooling, substrate, and split.

papers.title: SilencioMA: A single compound that targets both MAPT and APP as a potential disease modifying therapeutic for Alzheimer's Disease
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's Disease (AD) is the most common age-related neurodegenerative disease and the leading cause of dementia worldwide. AD pathogenesis involves aggregation of amyloid-beta (A{beta}), produced from amyloidogenic proteolytic processing of Amyloid Precursor Protein (APP), and accumulation of misfolded, pathological tau (Microtubule Associated Protein Tau, MAPT). Current efforts focus on developing disease modifying therapeutics (DMTs) against single targets: A{beta} or tau. However, DMTs that concurrently target both tau and A{beta} are likely to have the greatest impact since they target both culprits of AD pathogenesis. Here we describe the development of SilencioMA, a single compound that targets both MAPT and APP messenger RNAs (mRNAs) based on silencing connected interfering oligonucleotides against MAPT and APP. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) administration of SilencioMA reduces A{beta} and tau and pathology after a single intracerebroventricular injection in 5XFAD/PS19 mice, an animal model of severe amyloidosis and tauopathy. SilencioMA does not rely on lipid nanoparticles or lipophilic conjugates for CSF administration. At the same time its modular design permits conjugation of ligands that facilitate transcytosis through the blood brain barrier, allowing systemic administration. Our findings provide proof-of-concept for a strategy that targets the dual A{beta} and tau pathologies of AD, and establishes a compelling foundation for further development of SilencioMA as a next-generation DMT for AD.

papers.title: AI-readiness criteria for biomedical data in functional genomics and clinical medicine
papers.abstract: Biomedical research is rapidly adopting artificial intelligence (AI). Yet the inherent complexity of biomedical data preparation requires implementing actionable, robust criteria for ethical and explainable AI (XAI) at the "pre-model" stage, encompassing data acquisition, detailed transformations, and ethical governance. Simple conformance to FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) Principles is insufficient. Here, we define criteria and practices for reliable AI-readiness of biomedical data, developed by the NIH Bridge to Artificial Intelligence (Bridge2AI) Standards Working Group across seven core dimensions of dataset AI-readiness: FAIRness, Provenance, Characterization, Ethics, Pre-model Explainability, Sustainability, and Computability. Conformance to these criteria provides a basis for pre-model scientific rigor and ethical integrity, mitigating downstream risks of bias and error before AI modeling. We apply and evaluate these standards across all four Bridge2AI flagship datasets, spanning functional genomics to clinical medicine, and encode them in machine-actionable metadata bound to the datasets. This framework sets a benchmark for preparing ethical, reusable datasets in biomedical AI and provides standardized methods for reliable pre-model data evaluation.

papers.title: Integrated Genomic and Transcriptomic Profiling Reveals Distinct Biological Programs and Therapeutic Opportunities in Cancer of Unknown Primary
papers.abstract: BackgroundCancer of unknown primary (CUP) is a metastatic, heterogeneous malignancy accounting for 2-5% of cancer diagnoses globally. Failure to identify the primary site precludes tumor-type-specific therapy and, together with an aggressive clinical course, contributes to poor survival. The biological mechanisms driving these behaviors remain poorly understood. A deeper understanding of CUP biology is therefore essential to improve diagnostic precision and therapeutic strategies. To address this knowledge gap, we comprehensively characterized the multi-omics landscape of CUP and identified biological and potentially therapeutic targets beyond tissue-of-origin (ToO) assignment. MethodsWhole-genome sequencing (WGS) data from 283 CUP patients were analyzed for ToO predictions, mutational signatures, driver alterations, genetic immune escape (GIE), and clinically actionable alterations. Matched RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) data from 79 cases were used to characterize functional gene expression signatures and define transcriptomic subtypes. Clinical, WGS, and RNA-seq data were integrated via weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA). ResultsHigh-confidence ToO predictions (likelihood >80%) were obtained for 58% of CUPs, most commonly predicting lung, gastrointestinal, and biliary tract origins. Mutational signatures clustering revealed four subgroups dominated by tobacco smoking, defective DNA mismatch repair (dMMR), UV exposure, and APOBEC activity, while a fifth group, comprising most tumors (n=169; 60%), showed mixed mutational processes. The cohort also frequently exhibited mutations in established cancer driver genes, including TP53, CDKN2A, KRAS, and epigenetic modifiers ARID1A, SMARCA4, and ARID2. GIE alterations occurred in 35% of tumors, mostly involving HLA-I genes. Transcriptomic profiling defined five subtypes with different degrees of immune infiltration, fibrosis, and tumor proliferation. These subtypes were not significantly associated with clinical or genomic features, indicating that the tumor microenvironment (TME) represents another layer of CUP heterogeneity. WGCNA further linked proliferative programs to cell-cycle, DNA-replication, and neuroendocrine features. WGS data identified potentially targetable alterations in 64% of the CUP patients. ConclusionsCUP comprises biologically heterogeneous tumors with diverse predicted origins, mutational histories, and TME subtypes. Transcriptomic profiling and integrated genomics suggest that immune escape and rapid proliferation contribute to the clinical aggressive behavior. Together, these findings provide a molecular framework for understanding CUP heterogeneity and support therapeutic stratification by both ToO predictions and tumor-specific molecular alterations.
authors: van de Wouw, Y. A. J.
van de Werken, H. J. G.

papers.title: Human-Agentic AI Collaboration Workflow for Trend Analysis of ChatGPT Applications in Healthcare
papers.abstract: BackgroundWith the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI), large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT have demonstrated strong potential to transform healthcare research and practice. However, LLMs are probabilistic and generate inherently variable outputs, which create risk and uncertainty in healthcare applications. Therefore, analyzing the current research landscape of ChatGPT applications is imperative to understand applied techniques and related concerns and to facilitate their practical integration into healthcare information systems. ObjectiveLeveraging LLM-based agentic AI with domain experts to analyze trends in ChatGPT healthcare applications and to examine the collaborative and interpretative capacities of LLM agents in broader contexts beyond narrowly defined topics. MethodsThe review used a systematic search of the PubMed and Web of Science databases, following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, and focused on ChatGPT applications, associated concerns, applied techniques, and usage factors. To support the review process, an adaptive, iterative LLM-based agentic AI with a human-in-the-loop mechanism was employed for automated metadata extraction, identification, classification, and knowledge synthesis. The extracted information was subsequently used for temporal and thematic analyses, citation network construction, and main-path analysis. ResultsAcross 192 papers, the review identified 511 ChatGPT application types, 690 concern items, and 368 influence usage factors distinct from traditional IT, achieving a metadata error rate of 1.04%. The human-agentic AI workflow enabled efficient synthesis of contextual information across studies, addressing the growing challenge of timely evidence integration in medical knowledge. The findings provide insights into the evolving trajectories of ChatGPT applications in healthcare and demonstrate the value of an expert-validated human-agentic AI workflow in supporting literature analysis and streamlining review processes. ConclusionThis review provides a comprehensive overview of emerging ChatGPT applications, associated concerns, applied techniques, and usage factors in healthcare. The study further provides meaningful insights into the operational mechanisms of agentic AI, demonstrating the potential of human-AI collaboration for medical informatics research.

papers.title: Evaluation of System One Models on Biomedical Texts
papers.abstract: Objective To compare the performance and cost of System One models (SOMs) with general-purpose large language models (LLMs) on biomedical tasks and evaluate confidence-based routing. Materials and Methods We evaluated three SOMs and three LLMs across seven datasets and eight endpoints covering question answering, error detection, structured extraction, and clinical-note assessment. Outcomes included task-specific performance, recorded inference cost and latency, and confidence calibration. Calibration data determined routing schemes and confidence thresholds to evaluate test predictions, with cost-matched random referral as a comparator. Results Claude Opus 5.5 had the highest primary performance on all eight endpoints. The strongest SOM, Jev, had competitive performance with the evaluated LLMs and cost less than 1% of Opus on most datasets. Three selected SOM-to-LLM routes reduced costs by 30.0%-71.7% relative to the receiving LLM, with modest reductions in performance. On one benchmark, SOM-to-SOM routing achieved 91.1% accuracy, compared with 82.3% and 82.2% for the individual models. Discussion SOMs offered favorable performance-cost tradeoffs for most tasks. The magnitude of the advantages depended on task structure and prompting requirements. Confidence-based routing between SOMs and LLMs can leverage complementary model strengths and offers additional flexibility in performance-cost tradeoffs. The price advantages offered by SOMs can facilitate experimentation and development of workflows. This warrants further evaluation on closed datasets. Conclusion For biomedical tasks with predefined choices, SOMs represent a competitive stand-alone or first-stage approach.

papers.title: Multi-Model Comparison of Deep and Classical Architectures for ECG Diagnostic Superclass Classification on PTB-XL
papers.abstract: Objective. It remains unclear which architecture best sorts 12-lead electrocardiograms into diagnostic superclasses, and whether added model complexity pays off. Methods. Using 21,375 PTB-XL records under one patient-level split, we compared a Mamba-style state space model, a residual convolutional network, a bidirectional long short-term memory network, a convolutional-recurrent network with attention, soft-voting ensembles of these networks, and MiniRocket features with LightGBM. Each record took the superclass of its highest-likelihood diagnostic code, and we scored saved predictions with paired patient-level bootstrap intervals. Results. No model clearly outperformed MiniRocket with LightGBM, which needs no graphics processor. The ensemble of the three deep models with the highest validation macro F1 score reached 0.656, against 0.645 for MiniRocket with LightGBM (difference +0.011, 95% confidence interval -0.007 to +0.031), and an ensemble of all four deep models reached 0.657. An exploratory ensemble, whose members we chose after seeing test results, reached 0.665 and was the only ensemble whose interval excluded zero (+0.021, 0.002 to 0.040); we regard that margin as optimistic. Hypertrophy was the hardest class (F1 0.33 to 0.41), and differences in its recall mostly reflected threshold placement. Conclusions. Under one shared split, deep ensembles added little over a classical pipeline. Significance. These results give biomedical informatics researchers a statistically grounded reference for judging whether complex models justify their cost on this benchmark. With one dataset, one split, one training seed per model, and no external validation, they do not show readiness for clinical use.

papers.title: Agentic AI versus pediatric emergency physicians for differential diagnosis of acutely ill and injured children
papers.abstract: Background Misdiagnosis and delayed diagnosis of children in pediatric emergency departments lead to complications, and are particularly problematic in settings with limited pediatric expertise. Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in diagnostic reasoning for adult emergency department patients, but utility for pediatric cases is largely untested. Methods Retrospective study of patients seen in the emergency department of a major urban pediatric academic medical center and subsequently admitted to the operating room or inpatient service. Records from 100 patients were randomly selected, stratified by age. We compared the accuracy of differential diagnoses (up to five, ranked by likelihood) generated by an LLM agent, Dr CaBot (one configuration with literature search, the other without), with those of four attending pediatric emergency medicine physicians (diagnosticians), all masked to outcome. Encounters were presented to diagnosticians stepwise across four touchpoints: triage, the initial physician evaluation (the a priori primary touchpoint), the full emergency department encounter, and the admission. Ground truth diagnosis was determined by two independent, board-certified pediatric emergency physicians (reviewers) based on the entire clinical encounter. The reviewers, masked to source, then assigned each differential a Bond score (0 to 5; 4 or above was high-scoring). Findings The median patient age was 4 years and 41% had a complex chronic condition. Bond score agreement between the two reviewers had a weighted kappa of 0.64. For the primary comparison at the initial physician evaluation touchpoint, the LLM agent and the diagnosticians both achieved high-scoring differentials in 95% of cases (difference 0%, 95%CI: -5.8, 5.8%). No differences were detected at the other touchpoints. Interpretation Dr CaBot and attending pediatric emergency medicine physicians showed similar performance in generating differential diagnoses from clinical documentation, suggesting potential as a diagnostic aid. Whether this performance improves care, particularly outside pediatric specialty centers, requires prospective evaluation.

papers.title: Genome-resolved metagenomics reveals population-dependent gut microbiome responses to albendazole-ivermectin treatment
papers.abstract: Soil-transmitted helminth control relies on mass anthelmintic treatment, yet helminth-anthelmintic-microbiome interactions and their role on treatment response remain poorly understood. We characterised the microbiome, resistome, and functional profiles of 858 paired stool metagenomes from 429 children treated with albendazole or a fixed-dose albendazole-ivermectin co-formulation in the ALIVE clinical trial in Ethiopia and Mozambique. Baseline microbiome composition differed more by country than infection status and was not associated with albendazole efficacy or adverse events. Co-formulation treatment, particularly three consecutive daily doses, was associated with depletion of Enterobacteriaceae, predominantly Escherichia coli, in Ethiopia, with reductions in E. coli-associated resistance genes and metabolic pathways. Genome-resolved analyses of over 22,000 high-quality metagenome-assembled genomes confirmed this depletion across multiple E. coli strain-level populations, linking taxonomic, resistome, and functional signals to one ecological event. These findings reveal an off-target effect of combination anthelmintic treatment relevant to large-scale deworming programmes and expand genomic resources for African gut microbiota.

papers.title: HLA-Resolve: Four-field HLA typing and MHC variant detection from long-read hybrid capture
papers.abstract: The major histocompatibility complex (MHC) is among the most polymorphic and difficult-to-genotype regions of the human genome. Accurate typing of its HLA genes, which encode antigen-presenting molecules, is critical for transplantation, pharmacogenomics, and disease-risk prediction. Long-read sequencing is increasingly used in HLA typing because of its ability to phase variants across long distances, but many long-read HLA typing workflows still rely on long-range PCR. Here, we present an end-to-end workflow for MHC genotyping that pairs hybrid capture with long-read sequencing on PacBio or Oxford Nanopore, using single-step enzymatic fragmentation and barcoding to enable automated library preparation. The hybrid capture panel enriches both classical and non-classical HLA Class I and Class II genes, as well as all 69 protein-coding MHC Class III genes. We introduce HLA-Resolve, a bioinformatic tool that types HLA genes from PacBio reads via phased full-gene sequence reconstruction, and we benchmark the capture assay and HLA-Resolve together across 32 geographically diverse samples. With PacBio data, variant calling achieved F1 scores of 99.8% for SNVs and 98.4% for indels against the Genome in a Bottle benchmark. HLA-Resolve showed 99.5% allele concordance with reference typings from the International Histocompatibility Working Group and the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium (HPRC) at three-field resolution and 90.5% at four-field resolution, outperforming three other open-source long-read HLA typers on our HiFi hybrid capture reads. The full-gene sequences reconstructed by HLA-Resolve showed zero edit distance to the corresponding HPRC assemblies in 95% of comparisons. HLA-Resolve also showed high accuracy with whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data, achieving 99.4% two-field concordance across 146 public PacBio WGS libraries and 99.5% three-field concordance across the 52 with full-resolution reference typings. Although developed for the MHC, the workflow is customizable to any gene set, providing a general framework for high-resolution genotyping.

papers.title: Prospective prediction of clinical trial outcomes from public evidence
papers.abstract: Predicting clinical trial outcomes requires interpreting biological and clinical evidence in the context of a specific intervention, population and study design. Here we test whether a general-purpose large language model (LLM) can predict trial outcomes from publicly available evidence. We introduce TrialDossier, which assembles standardized evidence dossiers, and TrialOutlook, which uses these dossiers with GPT-5 to estimate the probability that a trial meets its prespecified primary endpoint. Among 694 ongoing trials with results expected within six months of cohort assembly, 69 outcomes first disclosed after forecast recording had been adjudicated by 20 October 2026. TrialOutlook achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.819 (95% confidence interval, 0.708 to 0.914) and an average precision of 0.860. TrialOutlook correctly identified 27 of 29 failures (93.1%) and incorrectly classified 17 of 40 successes as failures. We further recorded forecasts for 5,809 ongoing trials associated with US-listed companies and established a public benchmark linking archived evidence and fixed forecasts to adjudicated outcomes as they become available.

papers.title: Virtual spatial transcriptomics links kidney histopathology to disease-associated molecular programs
papers.abstract: Introduction: Spatial transcriptomics can resolve compartment-specific molecular programs in kidney disease, but its cost and technical requirements limit its use in clinical diagnostics and in large biopsy archives. Predicting spatial gene expression from routine histology with artificial intelligence could extend molecular characterization to existing clinically annotated kidney tissue collections. Methods: We adapted DeepSpot-M, a pretrained multimodal foundation model that predicts spatial gene expression from histology, using paired hematoxylin and eosin images and Visium spatial transcriptomics from 209 Kidney Precision Medicine Project (KPMP) participants. We evaluated virtual profiles in held-out human biopsies, associated them with histopathologic and biochemical injury markers in 567 rats with defined nephrotoxin exposures from a public toxicogenomics database, and generated a virtual atlas from 1,534 histology slides of 476 additional KPMP participants. Results: Kidney-specific adaptation of DeepSpot-M doubled the mean Pearson correlation of each model's 1,000 best-predicted genes (0.43 versus 0.22) and exceeded recent foundation models. Virtual profiles preserved the direction of all 13 disease-marker differences in measured expression, including tubular injury, maladaptive repair, gluconeogenesis, and fibrosis-associated programs. All 11 measured associations between molecular programs and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) were also preserved. Without rat-specific training, a virtual injury score distinguished moderate or severe histopathologic lesions (area under the curve, 0.85) and at least twofold blood urea nitrogen elevation (0.82). In our atlas of 5.46 million virtual spots, higher proximal tubule program scores were associated with higher eGFR (partial r, 0.32) and less interstitial fibrosis (-0.57), and program-pathology associations agreed with those of measured Visium profiles in independent participants (Spearman rho, 0.64). Conclusions: Kidney-adapted virtual spatial transcriptomics links histology-derived molecular programs to experimental renal injury and human clinical and histologic phenotypes. Our approach enables spatial molecular analyses in routine biopsy histology, which could help decipher disease-associated pathways in existing biopsy archives.

papers.title: Fine-tuned encoders, generative large language models and typed decisions for classifying findings in chest CT reports: paired English-Japanese internal testing and external testing on naturally written Japanese reports
papers.abstract: Purpose: To compare fine-tuned encoders, generative large language models (LLMs) and typed decisions (per-finding yes/no questions answered with a probability) for classifying 18 findings in chest CT reports, and to identify when typed decisions help. Methods: This retrospective study used public data. The internal test set comprised 150 CT-RATE reports with paired Japanese translations at three quality levels; the external test set, 243 naturally written Japanese reports with human annotations (RR-Findings). We compared ModernBERT encoders fine-tuned on 20,444 reports, generative LLMs (gpt-6-luna, Qwen3.8-27B, MedGemma), and typed decisions with Jev, the Decisions API and Qwen. Thresholds fixed on 450 development reports were applied unchanged externally. The primary metric was micro-F1; case-level paired bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated for 11 internal comparisons. Results: Encoders were best internally (English 0.9853; radiologist-checked Japanese 0.9576) and exceeded Jev (differences 0.0367, 95% CI 0.0258-0.0484; 0.0336, 0.0215-0.0464). Externally, Jev (0.8844) lay within the encoder seed range (0.8656-0.9144), exceeded the three generative conditions tested externally (best 0.8564) and the Decisions API (0.8177), and had the smallest internal-to-external decrease (-0.0396). An encoder trained on 2,044 reports reached 0.8226 externally. Typed-versus-generated differences changed direction across models and test sets. At a fixed threshold of 0.5, Jev fell to 0.7753 externally. Conclusion: Fine-tuned encoders performed best with ample in-distribution labels. Although threshold-dependent, Jev, with thresholds fitted on only 450 labeled reports, fell within the encoder seed range externally and exceeded the generative LLMs and an encoder trained on 2,044 reports, making it an option when labels are scarce.
